title: Linking argparse Values to Path Objects
body: File paths received via `argparse` are initially strings. By converting this value into a `Path` object—such as `Path(args.input)`—you can more easily work with path information, such as the filename, extension, parent folder, and whether the file exists.
detail: CLI tools are typically run like this: python tool.py --input data.txt --output out/result.txt. In this case, args.input and args.output are passed as strings. While you can use them as strings, converting them to Path objects allows you to naturally use functions such as `input_path.exists()`, `input_path.suffix`, and `output_path.parent`. As a beginner, it’s a good idea to get into the habit of treating paths not just as simple strings, but as objects for working with the file system.

title: Checking Input Using `exists` and `suffix`
body: exists() reports only that a path exists at check time and is also true for a directory. For file input, use is_file() and still handle read errors. suffix is only a hint for choosing a parser; it does not prove that the content is valid JSON or CSV.
examples: if not input_path.exists(): raise SystemExit('File not found')
if input_path.suffix != '.txt': raise SystemExit('Only .txt files are allowed')

title: read_text, write_text, mkdir flow
body: read_text and write_text load or write a whole text file, so consider memory for large files. mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) can prepare parents but still fails for a conflicting file or insufficient permissions. Define encoding and overwrite policy explicitly.

title: Basic Workflow of the CLI for Processing Actual Files
body: The actual file-processing CLI is easier to understand if broken down into the following steps: parsing arguments, converting paths, validating input, reading files, processing them, creating an output folder, and saving the results. This step brings together the argparse, pathlib, regex, CSV, and JSON concepts we learned earlier.
detail: At first, it’s easy to write all the code in a single file. However, if you plan to use it repeatedly as a tool, it’s better to break the code into separate sections. `parse_args()` reads the command-line arguments, `Path(args.input)` creates a path object, and `exists()` checks for the input. Next, you can retrieve data using `read_text()` or by reading CSV/JSON files, perform the necessary processing, and then save the results using `write_text()` or by saving to a CSV file. Once you get the hang of this structure, you can turn small automation scripts into actual tools.
examples: parse_args() -> Path conversion -> exists() -> read_text() -> write_text()
